GRADES 5 – 7  ·  COMPUTER SCIENCE
A Scrollytelling Lesson

How Computers
Actually Work

Every laptop, phone, console, and smart device runs on the same simple idea. Scroll down to take it apart, piece by piece, and see what is really happening inside the machine.

Scroll to begin ↓
Part 1

What Is a Computer?

A computer is a machine that follows instructions. It is not "smart" the way a person is. It does not understand the world. It just carries out carefully written instructions, called programs, very quickly.

No matter how different they look, almost every digital device does the same four jobs over and over. A phone, a Chromebook, a PlayStation, a smart TV, even a traffic light controller all run on this one loop:

The loop that runs every computer: input, processing, storage, output

Watch it happen in a video game

🎮

Input

You press a button on the controller.

⚙

Processing

The system calculates what should happen next.

💾

Storage

It loads saved data, maps, and characters.

📺

Output

The screen changes, sound plays, the controller rumbles.

General vs. Special Purpose

A laptop is general-purpose: it writes essays, plays games, edits video, and browses the web. A calculator or a microwave's chip is special-purpose: it is built to do one narrow job really well.

Stop and Think

Your school Chromebook, a smart speaker, and a robot vacuum all look completely different. What is the one thing all three have in common that makes each one a computer?

Part 2

Hardware: The Physical Parts

Hardware means the parts of a computer you can physically touch: the screen, the chips, the wires, the memory, and the storage drives. If a computer were a living thing, hardware would be its body.

The motherboard: the road system

The motherboard is the main circuit board. The CPU, memory, storage, and graphics all attach to it or talk through it. A computer is not one magic box. It is a connected system of parts sending signals to each other, and the motherboard is the network of roads those signals travel on.

The CPU: the main processor

The CPU is often called the "brain" of the computer. That is a useful picture, but not perfect. A brain understands and feels. A CPU just follows instructions: calculating numbers, comparing values, moving data, and coordinating every other part, billions of times per second.

The CPU reads instructions, does the math, and sends the answer onward

RAM: short-term working memory

RAM is fast, temporary memory. It holds whatever the computer is using right now. When you turn the power off, RAM forgets everything.

Think of RAM as a desk. The bigger your desk, the more books, papers, and supplies you can spread out at once. A small desk means you keep putting things away and pulling them back out, which slows you down. That is why a computer with too little RAM feels sluggish.
RAM holds the active pieces; storage keeps the full copy

Storage: long-term memory

Storage saves your files, apps, photos, and games even after the power is off. A hard disk drive (HDD) uses spinning magnetic disks. A solid-state drive (SSD) uses flash memory with no moving parts, so it is usually much faster. That speed is why the PlayStation 5 uses a high-speed SSD to load games quickly.

GPU: the graphics processor

The GPU is built to do many similar math problems at the same time. That is perfect for drawing 3D worlds, lighting, shadows, and explosions. A CPU is a clever all-rounder; a GPU is a team of thousands of workers all solving simple problems at once.

Input and output devices

⌨

Input

Keyboard, mouse, touchscreen, microphone, camera, game controller, VR sensors.

🖥

Output

Monitor, TV, speakers, headphones, printer, controller rumble, LED lights.

🔌

Ports

USB, HDMI, Ethernet, Bluetooth, and Wi-Fi connect a computer to other devices.

Quick Check

You turn off your console. What disappears, and what stays?

Part 3

Software: The Instructions

Software is the set of instructions and data that tells the hardware what to do. If hardware is the body, software is everything the body has been told to do.

The operating system runs the show

The operating system (OS) is the main software that manages the whole machine. Windows, macOS, ChromeOS, Android, iOS, and the system software inside a PlayStation or Switch are all operating systems. The OS is the first program to start when you power on, and it manages everything after that:

⚙

Hardware

Controls the CPU, memory, storage, and devices.

📱

Apps

Loads programs and gives them time to run safely.

📁

Files

Creates, names, saves, and organizes your data.

🔐

Security

Manages passwords, permissions, and updates.

Software sits in layers: your apps talk to the OS, and the OS talks to the hardware

Other kinds of software

A driver helps the OS talk to a specific device, like a printer. Firmware is software built right into a piece of hardware on a chip, telling it how to start up and do its basic job. Routers, controllers, and cameras all have firmware.

Stop and Think

Right now your device might be playing music, downloading a file, and showing this page all at once. Something has to decide who gets to use the CPU and when. Which piece of software is doing that job?

Part 4

Binary: The Computer's Language

Deep inside, a computer is made of billions of tiny switches that are either on or off. That is why computers use binary, a number system with only two symbols: 0 and 1.

A single 0 or 1 is called a bit. It can mean off or on, false or true, no or yes. String 8 bits together and you get a byte, which is enough to represent a single letter.

Patterns of 0s and 1s become letters, numbers, colors, and sounds

How can just two symbols build everything? Computers use patterns of bits to represent numbers, letters, colors, sounds, images, video, and whole game worlds. The computer never "sees" a dragon or a castle. It stores patterns of numbers, and software turns those numbers into pictures, sound, and motion.

Try It: Count in Binary

Binary place values double each time: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. To make the number 5, turn on the 4 and the 1: 00000101, because 4 + 1 = 5.

Quick Check

How many bits are in one byte?

Part 5

Data, Algorithms, and Programs

Data is any information a computer can store and process: your name in a form, a saved game, a photo, a score, a message to a friend.

Files and folders

A file is a saved collection of data, like photo.jpg or essay.docx. A folder is a container that organizes files. The ending after the dot, called the file extension, tells the OS what kind of data is inside and which app should open it.

Algorithms: step-by-step recipes

An algorithm is a step-by-step method for solving a problem. A program is an algorithm written in a language a computer can run. Making a sandwich is an algorithm. So is making a game character jump:

A jump is just a clear list of steps the CPU repeats many times a second

People write programs in programming languages such as Python, JavaScript, Scratch, C++, and Java. Each is good for different jobs: Python is friendly for beginners, JavaScript powers websites, and C++ is common in game engines.

Quick Check

What is the difference between an algorithm and a program?

Part 6

What Happens When You Press Power

Turning on a computer kicks off a fast, fixed sequence of steps called booting up.

Power on, firmware checks the hardware, the OS loads into RAM, and you reach your home screen
Stop and Think

The operating system lives in storage when the power is off, but it has to be running in RAM to actually manage the computer. So how does it get from storage into RAM if the OS is not running yet? (Hint: which step in the sequence above does that job?)

Part 7

Networks and the Internet

A network is a group of connected computers. Your home Wi-Fi is a small network. The internet is a giant network of networks that connects computers all over the world.

DNS: the internet's phonebook

People like names such as example.com. Computers use numbers called IP addresses. The DNS translates the name you type into the number the machines actually use.

DNS turns a human-friendly name into a machine-friendly number

Packets: messages cut into pieces

Information sent across the internet is broken into small chunks called packets. Each packet carries a piece of the message plus a label telling the receiver how to put it back together. They can take different routes and still arrive correctly.

Packets split up, travel separate paths, and reassemble at the other end

The web is not the internet

People mix these up, but they are different. The internet is the global network of roads. The World Wide Web is one delivery service that uses those roads. Email, video calls, online games, and app updates all use the internet too, not just the web.

The internet is the road system. The web is one kind of delivery truck. Plenty of other vehicles use the same roads.
Quick Check

Why is information broken into packets before being sent?

Part 8

A Quick History of Computers

Computers did not appear overnight. They grew over centuries as people tried to calculate faster, store information, and connect to each other.

From counting beads to a console in your living room

The pattern is shrinking parts and growing power. Early machines used giant vacuum tubes as switches. The transistor made switches smaller and more reliable. The integrated circuit packed many components onto one chip, and the microprocessor put the whole CPU on a single chip. A modern phone chip holds billions of tiny switches that ENIAC could never have fit in a building.

A Game Console Is a Computer

A PlayStation 5 has a CPU, a GPU, 16 GB of memory, an SSD, an operating system, a network connection, input devices, and output devices. It is not separate from computer science. It is computer science you can hold.

Quick Check

What replaced large, hot vacuum tubes and helped computers shrink?

Part 9

Putting It Together: Inside a Video Game

A video game uses almost every part of a computer at once, which makes it the perfect way to see the whole system working together.

Most games run a repeating cycle called the game loop. It can run 30, 60, or even 120 times every second. That number is the frame rate, measured in frames per second, or FPS. Higher FPS looks smoother but demands more processing power.

The game loop: every frame reads your input, updates the world, then draws and plays it

In an online game, your system also sends data over the internet: your position, your actions, your score. Because messages take time to travel, online games must handle delay, called latency. That delay is what players call lag.

Stop and Think

Your friend has a powerful new console but still lags badly in an online match. Their hardware is excellent. Trace the path your game data travels and name what part of the system is most likely causing the lag.

AI Is Not Magic

Game enemies and modern AI both run on regular computers using data, algorithms, and processors. AI can be useful, but it can also make confident mistakes. People still need to check evidence, sources, and context. The machine processes patterns; it does not understand them.
